nodes.content: Enable zero-shot voice conversion across unseen tonal languages while transferring speaker identity without altering lexical tone or prosody.
requirements: Keep lexical-tone error within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech, preserving source intonation and rhythm.
Achieve 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance using evaluators independent of training.

nodes.content: Use language-agnostic acoustic units, locked source F0 and timing, and reference-conditioned spectral diffusion to transfer target timbre.
Can source-F0 locking prevent lexical-tone drift during reference-conditioned timbre diffusion in unseen tonal languages?
On held-out Yoruba and Thai, F0 locking limits tone error rate increase to ≤2 percentage points versus unconverted speech.
Convert held-out Yoruba and Thai speech with locked versus unlocked F0; independently score lexical-tone error against unconverted speech.
Independent annotators measured Yoruba/Thai tone errors of 7.4%/9.1% unconverted, 8.6%/10.5% F0-locked, and 13.2%/15.0% unlocked.
Retain source-F0 locking: Yoruba/Thai tone-error increases were 1.2/1.4 percentage points, versus 5.8/5.9 without locking.
With F0 locking retained, benchmark target-speaker acceptance against 90% at 1% FAR using independent verifiers; audit Yoruba/Thai rhythm.
Run frozen ECAPA-TDNN and ResNet speaker verifiers on converted Yoruba/Thai utterances; calibrate each at 1% FAR on disjoint speakers.
Yoruba–Thai verification report containing per-language ECAPA-TDNN and ResNet acceptance rates, 1% FAR calibration, and disjoint-speaker trial lists.
Independently replay the report’s trial lists to verify 1% FAR calibration, per-language acceptance, and disjoint-speaker evaluation.
Independent replay confirmed Yoruba/Thai target acceptance of 92.1%/90.7% (ECAPA) and 91.4%/90.2% (ResNet), each at 1% FAR.
On held-out Vietnamese creaky tones, F0 locking with source-voicing masks keeps tone-error increases within 2 percentage points.
Blinded annotators compare tone errors in held-out Vietnamese creaky-tone, F0-locked conversions with versus without source-voicing masks against unconverted speech.
Blinded annotators found Vietnamese creaky-tone errors of 8.3% unconverted, 12.0% F0-locked with masks, versus 14.6% without masks.
Augment F0-locked diffusion with source-derived glottal-pulse and aperiodicity tracks to preserve Vietnamese creaky tones while transferring reference timbre.
Train pulse-conditioned diffusion; benchmark Vietnamese/Yoruba/Thai tone drift ≤2 points, rhythm preservation, and independent-verifier acceptance ≥90% at 1% FAR.
Reuse the report’s Yoruba/Thai trials, add Vietnamese trials, and measure pulse-conditioned tone errors, syllable-duration MAE, and 1%-FAR acceptance.
Pulse-conditioned benchmark report with Vietnamese/Yoruba/Thai tone-error deltas, syllable-duration MAE, independent-verifier acceptance at 1% FAR, and trial manifests.
Audit benchmark report manifests; compare F0-only and pulse-conditioned conversions on tone drift, duration MAE, and 1%-FAR independent-verifier acceptance.
Vietnamese tone error: F0-only 12.0%, pulse-conditioned 9.8%, baseline 8.3%; pulse-conditioned duration MAE 12 ms, independent-verifier acceptance 91.2% at 1% FAR.
Adopt pulse conditioning for Vietnamese and retain verified F0-locked Yoruba/Thai conversions; Vietnamese tone drift falls to 1.5 points.
Can source-pulse conditioning preserve Vietnamese creaky-tone cues without leaking source-speaker identity into converted speech?
With pulse conditioning, Vietnamese tone-error drift stays ≤2 points while source-speaker acceptance remains ≤5% at 1% FAR.
On held-out Vietnamese pairs, independently score pulse-conditioned tone-error drift and source-speaker acceptance at 1% FAR.
Vietnamese tone-error drift was 1.5 points, but independent source-speaker verification accepted 11.6% of conversions at 1% FAR.
Speaker-adversarial pulse normalization reduces Vietnamese source-speaker acceptance from 11.6% to ≤5% at 1% FAR while maintaining ≤2-point tone drift.
Train speaker-adversarial pulse normalizer; compare held-out Vietnamese tone drift and independent source-speaker acceptance against unnormalized conversions at 1% FAR.
Normalized pulses reduced Vietnamese source-speaker acceptance from 11.6% to 3.8% at 1% FAR; tone-error drift remained 1.7 points.
Condition a language-agnostic timbre decoder on speaker-adversarial normalized pulses and source-aligned duration tokens, with target-only reference embeddings.
Will source-aligned duration tokens preserve unseen-language rhythm when target references speak substantially faster than source utterances?
Pair Vietnamese sources with ≥30%-faster references; compare normalized-pulse duration-token decoding against F0-plus-voicing-mask decoding on duration MAE and tone-error drift.
With ≥30%-faster references, masked-F0 drift was 1.8 versus 3.7 points previously; duration MAE was 18 versus pulse-token 12 ms.
Retain pulse tokens for rhythm; reconsider masked-F0 only with ≥30%-faster references, given 1.8-point versus prior 3.7-point tone drift.
Across held-out Yoruba, Thai, and Vietnamese with ≥30%-faster references, duration tokens keep syllable-duration MAE ≤15 ms.
Using retained pulse-duration tokens, test ≥30%-faster references across Yoruba, Thai, and Vietnamese for ≤15-ms syllable-duration MAE.
Using r1’s disjoint-speaker Yoruba/Thai trials, add Vietnamese and ≥30%-faster references; measure pulse-token syllable-duration MAE per language.
Fast-reference rhythm audit with disjoint-speaker trial manifests and per-language pulse-token syllable-duration MAE for Yoruba, Thai, and Vietnamese.
Audit r3’s disjoint-speaker manifests and ≥30%-faster pairings; independently reannotate syllables and recompute each language’s MAE against 15 ms.
Independent reannotation found pulse-token syllable-duration MAE of 13/14/12 ms for Yoruba/Thai/Vietnamese with ≥30%-faster references.
Audit r3 duration measurements and replay fast-reference trials for source-F0 deviation, tone drift, and independent-verifier acceptance at 1% FAR.
With ≥30%-faster Thai references, independent-verifier target acceptance fell to 86.7% at 1% FAR despite 14-ms duration MAE.
Retain duration tokens for 14-ms Thai rhythm, but defer fast-reference deployment: target acceptance is 86.7% at 1% FAR.
Train tempo-invariant target-speaker embeddings with time-stretched references, retaining source duration tokens and normalized pulses during timbre decoding.
Can tempo-invariant speaker embeddings restore Thai target acceptance with ≥30%-faster references without disturbing source duration or tone?
With ≥30%-faster references, tempo-invariant embeddings raise Thai acceptance to ≥90% at 1% FAR, preserving ≤15-ms MAE and ≤2-point tone drift.
On ≥30%-faster Thai trials, compare tempo-invariant versus original embeddings; measure independent-verifier acceptance at 1% FAR, duration MAE, and tone-error drift.
Thai fast-reference acceptance rose from 86.7% to 89.1% at 1% FAR; duration MAE was 14 ms, tone drift 1.6 points.
Contrastive target-speaker fine-tuning yields ≥90% Thai fast-reference acceptance at 1% FAR, ≤15-ms duration MAE, and ≤2-point tone drift.
Fine-tune tempo-invariant embeddings contrastively; on fast-reference Thai trials, independently assess target acceptance, duration MAE, and tone drift.
Contrastive fine-tuning achieved 91.0% Thai fast-reference target acceptance at 1% FAR, 14-ms duration MAE, and 1.7-point tone drift.
Advance contrastively tuned embeddings for Thai fast-reference conversion: acceptance recovered to 91.0%, with 14-ms rhythm MAE and 1.7-point tone drift.
Benchmark contrastively tuned embeddings across held-out tonal languages: ≤2-point tone drift, ≤15-ms duration MAE, ≥90% independent-verifier acceptance at 1% FAR.
Reprocess r2 trials and r3 fast-reference manifests with contrastively tuned embeddings; independently score tone drift, duration MAE, and 1%-FAR acceptance.
Cross-language validation report listing Yoruba/Thai/Vietnamese trial manifests, tone-error baselines and deltas, duration MAE, and independent 1%-FAR acceptance.
Audit r4 manifests for unseen-language separation; independently recompute per-language tone drift, duration MAE, and calibrated 1%-FAR target acceptance.
Independent r4 audit, Yoruba/Thai/Vietnamese: tone drift 1.2/1.7/1.7 points; duration MAE 13/14/12 ms; target acceptance 92.0/91.0/90.5% at 1% FAR.
Adopt contrastively tuned pulse-duration conversion for the evaluated languages; independent audits meet tone, rhythm, and target-verification thresholds.
